sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Long-term follow-up after low-dose rate brachytherapy and ultra-fractionated radiotherapy for localised prostate cancer has demonstrated impressive survival statistics with low toxicity profiles. Superiority between the two treatments has not been shown, with a lack of randomised data comparing the two. Emerging studies have shown a benefit of adding a rectal spacer gel to sit between the prostate and anterior rectal wall to further reduce toxicity following radiotherapeutic treatments. Further randomised studies are, however, recommended to support this data. To the best of our knowledge, the LDR BURST Trial is the first randomised controlled study to compare the toxicity and survival outcomes of low dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy against ultra-hypofractionated external beam radiotherapy with a spacer gel in situ.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: This parallel group interventional study sets out to randomise 220 participants with Cambridge Prognostic Groups 1–3 prostate cancer to either LDR brachytherapy with a rectal spacer gel versus external five fraction ultra-fractionated radiotherapy (total dose 36.25 Gy) on a 1:1 basis. The primary outcome is detection of a minimally important difference using the validated Expanded Prostate Index Composite 26 (EPIC-26) questionnaire. Secondary outcomes include further validated patient-reported questionnaires, physician-reported adverse events and survival outcomes.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: The LDR BURST study has received Health Research Authority (HRA) and Health and Care Research Wales (HCRW) approval (reference 25/LO/047). All participants will provide informed consent prior to participation. Findings from this study will be disseminated through presentations at national and international conferences and publication in peer-reviewed journals.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: The LDR BURST is the first randomised controlled trial to compare the toxicities of low dose rate brachytherapy with a rectal spacer gel against five fraction ultra-hypofractionated radiotherapy with a spacer gel.

Our limitations include the following: (1) a single-centre approach. (2) There is no control group in this study that omits the use of rectal spacer gel. Patients may, however, decline the spacer gel and therefore can be included in a subcohort analysis.
Our strengths include the following: (1) randomised data. (2) Large cohort in each treatment arm with a long follow-up period. (3) Patient and clinician-reported outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In an era of advancing technology and novel therapeutic techniques, the radical treatment options for localised prostate cancer have never been greater. To date, there is no level 1 evidence to show superiority in survival outcomes when comparing external beam radiotherapy (EBRT), brachytherapy or a radical prostatectomy.1 Clinicians therefore require robust data to educate patients on the benefits and trade-offs of potential treatment-related toxicities.

Low dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy, a form of interventional radiotherapy, is a day-case procedure that entails permanent implantation of radioactive iodine-125 seeds into the prostate gland.2 In contrast to high dose rate brachytherapy, which delivers large fraction sizes (>12 Gy/hour) over two implants via temporary catheters, LDR brachytherapy delivers continuous high dose radiation locally, following a single implant. With a half-life of 60 days, radiation is slowly deposited into the gland over the coming months. LDR brachytherapy treatment has long-term data on efficacy, toxicity and patient-reported quality of life.36

Prostate LDR brachytherapy is a highly technical skill, influenced by operator expertise, intervention reproducibility and resource availability that can be reflected within frameworks such as the COMIRI complexity index.7 The National Institute for Healthcare and Clinical Excellence (NICE) has recommended the use of LDR brachytherapy for many years either as a monotherapy or in combination with ADT±EBRT (ADT, androgen deprivation therapy) for men with low, intermediate and high risk localised prostate cancer.8 During the 25 year period of performing LDR brachytherapy at the Royal Surrey County Hospital, we have captured long-term clinical follow-up data to monitor survival outcomes and toxicity effects with the use of validated questionnaires.911 We have treated over 6000 men with LDR brachytherapy since 1999. The 4D LDR brachytherapy technique has evolved from pioneering work at the Royal Surrey Urology department delivering a cost-effective treatment modality for localised prostate cancer with improved dosimetry and clinical outcomes since 2009.914

EBRT is an alternative therapeutic option that has demonstrated efficacy across all prostate cancer risk groups. The CHHIP trial revolutionised EBRT delivery, demonstrating the traditional 7-and-a-half-week regimen could be safely and effectively shortened to daily treatment (Monday–Friday) over 4 weeks.15 The low alpha/beta ratio of prostate cancers, relative to healthy surrounding tissue, makes hypofractionation (delivering a dose of more than 2 Gy per fraction) an attractive option that takes advantage of its increased sensitivity to dose per fraction. There is also a compelling economic argument for treating prostate cancer using hypofractionation. Ultra-hypofractionation, also known as stereotactic body radiotherapy treatment (SBRT), delivers more than 5 Gy per treatment fraction. This allows for even shorter treatment regimens to be delivered; however, there were concerns it may cause an increase in acute toxicity compared with moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy. The PACE-B trial provided level I evidence demonstrating non-inferiority of a five-fraction SBRT regimen to a moderately hypofractionated 20-fraction radiotherapy treatment, with comparable toxicity data using patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and clinician-reported outcomes.16

Collectively, 4D Brachytherapy and SBRT have shown excellent results in the treatment of prostate cancer with acceptable toxicity levels.17 Further research is, however, needed to optimise the low treatment-related toxicities. An area of interest in the radiotherapeutic field is the growing data supporting the benefits of rectal spacer gels in reducing patient toxicity and improving dosimetric parameters.1821 These resorbable gels increase the distance between the prostate and the patient’s anterior rectum, protecting the rectum from the unwanted exit dose from the prostate radiotherapy. Further studies within a randomised setting are therefore encouraged by NICE to validate these positive findings.22

sec.title: Trial objectives and end points
sec.p: The LDR BURST study sets out to compare the treatment-related toxicity of SBRT against LDR brachytherapy in men with Cambridge Prognostic Groups 1–3 prostate cancer with a rectal spacer gel. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first randomised control trial to compare these treatment modalities with a rectal spacer gel.

sec.title: Primary objective and endpoint
sec.p: The primary objective is assessment of patient-reported toxicity after SBRT or LDR brachytherapy with a rectal spacing gel using the Expanded Prostate Index Composite 26 (EPIC-26) questionnaire. Our hypothesis is that the acute (up to 3 months) and late (at 5 years) toxicity after SBRT will not be significantly different to that after LDR brachytherapy. PICO criteria are as follows:
P (Population) Eligible men with low to intermediate risk prostate cancer.
I (Intervention) SBRT plus HA rectal spacer.
C (Comparator) LDR brachytherapy plus HA rectal spacer.
O (Outcome) Treatment-related toxicity and disease control.

The primary outcome is detection of a minimally important difference (MID) in EPIC-26 questionnaire scores relative to the pretreatment values (see pg 21, section 8.1 for definition). Acute toxicity (before 3 months) and toxicity at 5 years are the main time points of interest. EPIC-26 scores will be collected at 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months after treatment and then yearly up to the 5 year post-treatment time point.

The EPIC-26 questionnaire is a pre-eminent tool extensively characterised to measure health-related quality of life in men with localised prostate cancer.23 Our study is powered based on guidelines issued by the EPIC team to detect the MID in urinary, sexual and bowel function domains.24

The EPIC-26 score is a continuous variable that ranges from 0 to 100 with higher scores indicating better function. Because of skewness, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U tests are frequently used to detect MID relative to the pretreatment value. If the scores show a normal distribution, a t-test for the mean of the differences is more appropriate. Tests for proportions of cases with values above the MID are used to compare the effects between treatment groups. Regression analyses help identify factors associated with score changes throughout follow-up.

sec.title: Secondary objectives and endpoints
sec.p: The secondary objectives are as follows:
1. Patient-reported genitourinary, erectile potency and bowel toxicity following SBRT or LDR brachytherapy with a rectal spacer gel.

Our secondary outcomes will be measured using the International Index of Erectile Function 5-item questionnaire (IIEF-5), International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and the Vaizey Incontinence Score questionnaire.

The IPSS is made up of seven questions related to urinary voiding symptoms and one question on urinary bother.25 For voiding symptoms, a score of 0–7 indicates mild symptoms, 8–19 indicates moderate symptoms and 20–35 indicates severe symptoms, and the urinary bother scale ranges from 0 (delighted) to 6 (terrible). The IPSS is also used to assess patient eligibility for radiation treatments.

The IIEF-5, also known as the Sexual Health Inventory for Men (SHIM) score,26 characterises the severity of erectile dysfunction (ED) with lower scores indicating greater dysfunction (5–7 severe, 8–11 moderate, 12–16 mild-to-moderate, 17–21 mild, 22–25 no ED).
The Vaizey Incontinence Score27 is a general-purpose scale for faecal incontinence that ranges from 0 to 24 with higher scores representing worst incontinence.

2. Clinician-reported outcomes following treatment, grading the following domains; haematuria, dysuria, urinary frequency, urinary incontinence, urinary retention, urethral stricture, proctitis, diarrhoea, rectal haemorrhage, rectal fistula, constipation, ED and fatigue.

Physician-reported toxicity outcomes will be measured using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE V.5) guidelines. The adverse events are classified into grades based on severity as follows:

list-item.p: Grade 1: mild; asymptomatic or mild symptoms; clinical or diagnostic observations only; intervention not indicated.
Grade 2: moderate; minimal, local or non-invasive intervention indicated; limiting age-appropriate instrumental activities of daily living (ADL).
Grade 3: severe or medically significant but not immediately life-threatening; hospitalisation or prolongation of hospitalisation indicated; disabling; limiting self-care ADL.
Grade 4: life-threatening consequences; urgent intervention indicated.
Grade 5: death related to AE.

sec.p: The grade and timing of the adverse events are used to derive cumulative incidences for comparisons between treatment groups.

3. Treatment efficacy by estimation of freedom from treatment failure, either biochemical failure, clinical failure (commencement of ADT, clinical or radiographic evidence of local recurrence, or nodal or distant metastasis) 5 years post-treatment.
4. Disease-specific and overall survival are estimated by measuring time from treatment to death from prostate cancer and death from any cause, respectively.

Survival outcomes are time-to-event variables for relapse-free survival, cancer-specific survival and overall survival. Treatment relapse is defined as evidence of biochemical failure (three consecutive rises in the first 2 years following treatment or a rise in the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) value greater than 2 ng/mL over the nadir after 2 years), or clinical or radiographic evidence of local or distant progression. Post-treatment imaging is at the discretion of the treating clinician and not routine. Cancer-specific survival estimates the probability of death due to prostate cancer and overall survival the probability of death from any cause. Time will be measured from completion of radiotherapy and comparisons between groups made by Cox proportional hazards regression.

It is now recognised that following SBRT or LDR brachytherapy, a ‘PSA bounce’ (when a spike in a PSA level spontaneously resolves) can be seen, typically within the first 2 years after treatment.28 29 Therefore, biochemical failure within the first 24 months will be defined as three consecutive rises over at least a 6 month period. After 2 years post-treatment, the treatment failure definition will revert to the Phoenix definition, of the nadir PSA value +2 ng/mL.
5. Evaluate patient experience during their treatment pathway.

A small cohort of patients (aiming for 20 patients) will be asked about their experiences during the screening, consenting and treatment process. Within this cohort, we will also seek to interview patients who decline randomisation and come off the study. This qualitative piece of research, included within the Medical Doctorate, will help guide future patients and clinicians with discussions on the two standards of care treatment options offered within the National Health Service (NHS), management of their toxicities and possibly identify barriers to randomised control studies. Patient interviews will be audio recorded using an NHS password-protected computer. The manuscript will be uploaded onto NVivo software (with all patient identifiable data removed).

This qualitative work can be used in conjunction with the quality of life scoring within the validated questionnaires. Suitable participants for interview will be identified at their screening or 1 month follow-up appointment. Written consent will be obtained for their interview to be recorded on NHS password protected computers.

sec.title: Trial design
sec.p: This is a parallel group interventional study designed to understand the differences between stereotactic body radiotherapy and LDR brachytherapy with regard to patient-reported toxicity measured primarily by the EPIC-26 questionnaire.
The MID in EPIC-26 scores are known and both treatments are considered standard of care; therefore, the trial tests for equality between the two treatments.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The eligibility criteria follow those used by the PACE-B randomised study16 to facilitate comparisons on an effect of SBRT on treatment toxicity.

sec.title: Inclusion
sec.p: Inclusion criteria are:

list-item.p: Men aged≥18 years at randomisation.
The research subject must have capacity to sign a written informed consent document for the trial.
WHO performance status 0–2.
Gleason score 3+3 or 3+4.
PSA≤20 ng/mL (please note if the treating clinician determines ADT is required, this is an exclusion criterion). A PSA must be available within 60 days of randomisation.
Clinical and/or MRI stage T1c–T2c, N0-X, M0-X.

Histological confirmation of prostate adenocarcinoma within the last 18 months (unless on active surveillance). Patients who were on active surveillance should have an up-to-date MRI within 8 weeks of the decision to treat to confirm organ-confined disease.

sec.title: Exclusion
sec.p: Exclusion criteria are:

list-item.p: Previous malignancy within the last 2 years (except basal cell carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma of the skin), or if previous malignancy is expected to significantly compromise 10 year survival.
Patients under investigation for synchronous primary at the time of randomisation.
Prior pelvic radiotherapy.
Prior treatment with ADT or current need for ADT based on risk features.
Prostate cancer in greater than 50% of template biopsy cores or a significant maximum core length containing prostate cancer for which the treating clinician deems the patient would benefit from ADT.
Any prior active treatment for prostate cancer (patients previously on active surveillance are eligible if they meet all other eligibility criteria).
Life expectancy<10 years.

Hip prostheses or any other implants/hardware that introduce substantial CT artefacts making it challenging to delineate the target or organs at risk (OAR). This is to be assessed on a case-by-case basis with the available staging imaging.
Medical conditions likely to make radiotherapy inadvisable, for example, inflammatory bowel disease and significant urinary symptoms.
IPSS>15 points.
Anticoagulation with warfarin/bleeding tendency making fiducial placement, spacer gel insertion or brachytherapy unsafe in the opinion of the clinician.

Contraindications for Barrigel insertion such as previous documented allergic reaction to gel, previous rectal surgery or known rectal fistula. Note, patients who decline rectal spacer gel insertion will remain eligible for inclusion in the study and will be analysed as a predefined subcohort.
Participation in another concurrent treatment protocol for prostate cancer.

sec.title: Patient identification
sec.p: Patients suitable for the trial will be highlighted at their local prostate cancer MDT. Patients deemed eligible for all radical treatment options for their prostate cancer (surgery or radiotherapy) will be reviewed by the surgical and oncology team as per standard of care management. Should the patient express an interest in radiation treatment and be willing to be randomised to either radiation treatment arm (LDR brachytherapy or SBRT), an onward referral should be made to the trial team. Written patient information on the trial can be provided to the patient before meeting the trial team. Should the patient have a preference for which treatment arm they would prefer, then they will be offered this as standard of care (should they be deemed suitable by the treating clinician). If patients are willing to have either LDR brachytherapy or SBRT treatment, then they will undergo screening at their first trial appointment.

sec.title: Screening
sec.p: All men within the trial will have prostate cancer classified as Cambridge Prognostic Groups 1–3, corresponding to low to intermediate risk prostate cancer, as defined by NICE criteria.30 Patients will undergo a baseline urinary flow rate assessment, transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) and IPSS questionnaire as part of their eligibility assessment prior to randomisation. The urinary flow rate should be above 10 mL/s, as a figure less than this is suggestive of an obstructive prostate, likely requiring intervention such as a transurethral resection of the prostate. A TRUS is an important diagnostic tool as it demonstrates the size and shape of the prostate. Men with a prostate gland larger than 60 cc, or those with a large median lobe, are not good candidates for LDR brachytherapy and therefore are excluded from the trial, due to challenging dose distribution and increased risk of toxicity.

A PSA within 60 days of randomisation is required to be used as a baseline result. Any patients deemed high risk and therefore requiring hormonal treatment, as per local policy, alongside their radiotherapy, will be excluded from the study.
Patients not eligible for the trial will be offered an alternative standard of care option, and these patients will not be included in the final analysis.

sec.title: Consent
sec.p: Suitable participants interested in the LDR BURST trial will be given a patient information sheet (PIS) prior to consent. This information booklet will explain the details of the study, in layman terms, including the randomisation process, the advantages and disadvantages of the study and the follow-up procedure. The patient must have had at least 24 hours from reading the PIS, prior to obtaining informed consent. Ideally, the PIS will be given to the patient following their initial oncology review.

Only those who are trained and competent in consent, according to Good Clinical Practice, will be allowed to consent the patient for the study. Following randomisation and treatment allocation, the participant will then sign a Trust approved treatment-specific consent form that will highlight acute and late side effects of their assigned treatment. The treatment-specific consenting process may happen at a later date from randomisation but again will only be performed by those with the appropriate training and knowledge of the treatment and its side effects.

A participant will remain free to withdraw from the study at any point. On withdrawal of consent, they will be asked if they would be in agreement for their data to be stored for analysis (if appropriate), for example if a patient wishes to withdraw from the study 6 months following treatment.

Participants will be assumed to have capacity to consent unless they have a history of cognitive impairment or demonstrate concerns regarding capacity during their treatment work-up. In this case, capacity will need to be assessed on an individual basis. Patients deemed to lack capacity and who are unable to consent themselves to the study will be excluded from the study, as this may have implications with future symptom reporting.

Study questionnaires will be available electronically or in paper format. For participants who chose to fill their questionnaire out electronically, a copy will be sent to their personal email at each time point. Participants will consent to their contact details being stored on the research electronic data capture (REDCap) database system and to receive emails from the study group. Paper questionnaires will be given to the patient when they attend for their face-to-face appointment to fill out prior to their next appointment.

The study PIS, consent form and questionnaires will be written in plain English. Should a participant be unable to speak, read or write in English, then an official translator should be sought to translate the information, to help the patient make an informed decision. Follow-up consultations that take place over the phone may use telephone translation services.

sec.title: Randomisation
sec.p: Patients will be randomised within the study following informed consent. If the patient has read the PIS prior to their initial trial screening review and is happy to give their informed consent, then they can be randomised at their initial trial review or shortly afterwards to avoid any delay in their treatment pathway.

The study will use permuted block randomisation with two block sizes, stratification by the risk of relapse (low or intermediate), and equal (1:1) allocation. The allocation sequence is obtained using the R package ‘blockrand’.31 Trial co-ordinators responsible for randomisation will have no prior knowledge of the randomisation design, therefore negating selection bias per treatment arm.

sec.title: Method of randomisation
sec.p: Randomisation will be performed with the randomisation module of the REDCap platform (see section 9 on Data Handling). The module facilitates the execution of a preloaded allocation table. The statistician is the only member of the team with knowledge of the design of the allocation sequence. The sequence is therefore fully concealed from all other trial members.

A unique REDCap identifier is assigned to each patient by trial coordinators with access to a stand-alone database containing patient personal information. The unique identifier acts as a pseudonym that links back to NHS/Hospital numbers. Once eligibility criteria have been entered and met, the randomisation module is enabled. Allocation to the treatment arm is immediately recorded in the randomisation module and it is irrevocable. Patients, treating physicians and specialist nurses would be notified by post, email or telephone as appropriate. The database identifier is also the allocation number that can be accessed 24/7 by trial team members.
It is recommended that the radiotherapy treatment should start within 8 weeks of randomisation and must start by week 12.

sec.title: Blinding (allocation concealment)
sec.p: Blinding is not possible to either treating clinicians or trial participants given the difference in treatment delivery. Follow-up assessments for CTCAE grading and PROMs questionnaires data input will also be unblinded. On study closure, outcome assessors will be blinded when reviewing the primary and secondary outcomes, with the two treatment groups being renamed ‘Treatment 1’ and ‘Treatment 2’ during the analysis process.

sec.title: Baseline data
sec.p: Baseline data include all variables related to demography, assessment for radiotherapy, and eligibility criteria and/or outcomes analyses (table 1).

caption.title: The baseline data captured for each participant

tr.td: Biopsy detail (date, type, containers, core numbers, location, laterality, tumour size, invasion, Gleason)
Imaging detail (bone scan, MRI, CT, PET-CT)

sec.title: Trial assessments
sec.p: Baseline patient characteristics are assessed during the local MDT and participant information recorded in six data collection instruments (DCI). The baseline DCI capture demography, prior urological procedures, medical history, current assessment for radiotherapy, the EPIC-26 questionnaire, the IVI (IPSS, Vaizey faecal incontinence and IIEF-5) questionnaire, summary PROMs scores (populated from the questionnaires) and urodynamics. Treatment allocation takes place once eligibility criteria entered in the baseline DCI are met. The treatment date and treatment visit-related information is gathered followed by an initial assessment at 4 and 8 weeks after treatment completion for PROMs, treatment-related complications, concomitant medications or treatments and of urinary catheter use. Thereafter, follow-up assessments include PROMs, blood PSA measurements, clinical or radiographic evidence of tumour progression, use of salvage therapy and treatment-related complications or any additional medical or surgical treatment. Individual DCIs are used for detail of complications, use of concomitant medications or surgical treatment, withdrawal and for follow-up after further cancer therapy.

Alongside the primary data analysis, we will conduct a qualitative study to review the patients experience and attitude towards their respective radiation treatment. We will conduct a semistructured face-to-face or telephone interview. All patients will give their written consent for their interviews to be audio recorded. We hope to interview 20 patients in total, with five of these patients declining the study. The interviews will explore patients’ perceptions of the treatment pathway for each radiation technique and the protective rectal spacing gel. This data will be used within the Medical Doctorate awarded to the PI.

sec.title: SBRT radiotherapy planning
sec.p: The prescription dose is 36.25 Gy given in five fractions over 1–2 weeks (ie, daily or alternate daily at department discretion) delivered on linear accelerator. Patients undergoing treatment at the Royal Surrey County Hospital will be recommended to have fiducial markers inserted prior to their treatment; however, these are not mandatory for the study. Gold Anchor fiducial markers (Naslund Medical) will be inserted at the same appointment as their Barrigel rectal spacer insertion, to limit appointment burden and anaesthetic for each patient. An added advantage of using Gold anchor markers is their unique design that allows a thin needle (22–25 G) for implantation, minimising trauma and therefore allowing the patients planning CT scan to be expedited to as early as the same day, rather than wait 7 days postfiducial implant. This will therefore speed up the patient’s treatment pathway and again cut down appointment burden.3234

The clinical target volume (CTV) for low-risk patients (Gleason score≤6, T1–T2a or PSA<10 ng/mL) is the prostate only. For intermediate-risk patients (Gleason score 3+4, T2b or T2c or PSA 10–20 ng/mL), the CTV is the prostate plus a proximal 1 cm of seminal vesicles from insertion point in the superior–inferior plane. The planning target volume (PTV) is defined as the CTV plus a 5 mm isotropic margin with the exception of a 3 mm postmargin. The target dose objectives to meet are shown within table 2.

sec.title: LDR brachytherapy
sec.p: An outpatient assessment scan conducted prior to procedure determines the size of the prostate and shape using TRUS in the left lateral position. Five measurements are taken (prostate height, width, length and two para-sagittal lengths). Using the five prostatic measurements, a web-based nomogram calculates how many stranded and loose seeds will be required, which can then be ordered online. The stranded seeds are delivered in preloaded needles numbered in the correct order for implantation. The loose seeds are preloaded into Mick cartridges.

Seed implantation performed under general or spinal anaesthesia will follow the protocol laid out in the BXTA guidelines.35 All patients will undergo a postimplant CT scan for quality assurance within 24 hours to obtain early dosimetric feedback. Patients will receive prophylactic antibiotics postprocedure as per Trust guidance and 6 months of an alpha blocker, provided no contraindications, as per our standard of care.
Postoperative dosimetry aims: prescription dose 145 Gy.

list-item.p: Urethra V150%<10%.
Urethra D10%<150%.
Urethra D30%<130%.
Urethra mean<125%.
Rectum D2cc<100%.
Rectum D0.1cc<200 Gy.

sec.title: Hyaluronic acid rectal spacer: Barrigel
sec.p: Rectal spacing gels have been studied for several years in their addition to radiation treatment for prostate cancer to help reduce radiotherapy toxicities.36 Barrigel is a bio-degradable natural gel product. The spacer gel is inserted between the anterior rectal wall and the prostate, known as Denonvilliers’ fascia, to temporarily position the anterior rectal wall away from the prostate during radiotherapy for prostate cancer. The gel is slowly absorbed over 1–3 years, ensuring the prostate remains in a similar position for the treatment delivery. Barrigel was selected for this study due to its controlled deployment characteristics that allow the operator to shape the gel between the prostate±seminal vesicles and anterior rectal wall, allowing for reproducible separation.

To ameliorate the radiation effect on rectal tissue, all SBRT and LDR brachytherapy patients will undergo transperineal application of a Barrigel rectal spacer. Barrigel will be inserted under ultrasound guidance, by trained professionals only using an aseptic technique. The gel can be inserted under local or general anaesthetic. For patients receiving SBRT treatment, no general anaesthesia is required in their treatment work-up and therefore Barrigel will be inserted into Denonvilliers’ fascia under local anaesthetic following fiducial marker insertion. For patients receiving LDR brachytherapy, the gel will be inserted once all the radioactive seeds have been inserted during the same procedure. By incorporating the gel placement into each of these standard of care procedures for their respective treatments, this will cut down on treatment costs, room and staff availability as well as the need for additional anaesthetic.

sec.title: Barrigel insertion technique
sec.p: At least 3 mL of Barrigel inserted into Denovilliers space, aiming to create 1 cm separation from the prostate base to its apex from the anterior rectal wall. For intermediate risk SBRT patients, who will have the first 1 cm of seminal vesicle included within the CTV, additional Barrigel to create 1 cm separation from the seminal vesicle to the anterior rectal wall will be added. The gel will be inserted centrally, aiming for a symmetrical distribution on each side of the prostate under trans-rectal ultrasound supervision. Both sagittal and axial views on ultrasound should be assessed to check midline symmetry and adequate placement from base to apex, aiming for at least 1 cm separation.37 38

sec.title: Follow-up
sec.p: It is well documented that radiation toxicities are typically at their worst within the first 3 months following treatment.39 Patients will therefore have an intensive follow-up period following their respective treatments to assess their toxicity. Their end of treatment date will be noted as their day 0 with their first follow-up appointment 4 weeks later. Within the first 3 months following treatment, they will have two telephone consultations (at week 4 and week 8) in which they will have CTCAE scoring assessment of their side effects and will complete the EPIC-26 and IVI questionnaires. The patient will then have a face-to-face appointment at 3 months. If the patient underwent SBRT treatment, their follow-up will be with the treating oncologist. If the patient underwent brachytherapy, they will be followed up by the brachytherapy team. The patients first PSA will be recorded at 3 months after day 0. The interval between follow-up appointments will increase after the 3 month period as the acute toxicities wear off. However, unscheduled appointments can be booked if required.

sec.title: Withdrawal criteria
sec.p: The participant will be informed that they have the right to withdraw from the trial at any point. On withdrawal, they will be asked if they give their consent for their information to be stored on REDCap for analysis (if appropriate). The date at which the patient withdraws from the study will be recorded within their medical notes.

Should a patient withdraw from the study prior to starting treatment or the participant not complete their treatment, then they will be reviewed by the oncology team and an appropriate treatment plan will be made. Their data will not be included in the final analysis.

sec.title: End of trial
sec.p: The trial ends when the last accrued patient completes 5 years after treatment completion.

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: Detection of adverse events is an objective of the trial. These will be monitored using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE V.5) grading system40 and recorded in REDCap.

sec.title: Sample size calculation
sec.p: The study is powered to detect MID in EPIC-26 scales that range from 0 to 100 with higher values indicating better quality of life. The clinically relevant MID for the different domains was derived from distribution- and anchor-based analysis of a large population of men with localised prostate cancer.41
The MIDs (table 4) of the EPIC-26 domains of interest are as follows

sec.p: Based on an effect size of 0.5, power of 80% and a significance level of 5%, the sample size for a two-sided test ranges from 64 to 91, when any one or all of four EPIC-26 summary outcomes are tested, respectively (table 5). 110 subjects are required after adjustment for a drop out/non-response rate of 20%.

sec.p: Our statistical model has shown a total of 220 men are needed (110 participants per study arm) to demonstrate the desired effect size (factoring in a 20% drop out rate).

Additional non-spacer gel participants may be recruited beyond the predefined target sample size for inclusion in exploratory subcohort analyses. Recruitment of these participants will not alter the primary sample size calculation.

sec.title: Statistical analysis plan
sec.p: For patient-reported outcomes, the mean score differences at 5 years relative to baseline values will be compared with a t-test. If changes from baseline are not normally distributed, they will be compared with a Mann-Whitney U test.

The MID for each EPIC-26 domain is as follows: 5 points for the bowel domain, 6 points for urinary obstruction/irritative domain, 8 points for urinary incontinence domain and 11 points for the sexual function domain.41 For the IPSS, Vaizey and IIEF-5 scores, the MID will be defined as half of the SD of the pretreatment values and comparisons between treatment groups made using χ2 or Fisher’s exact tests as appropriate.

The grade and timing of the adverse events will be used to derive cumulative incidences from the hazard function in order to compare treatment groups. Statistical significance derived with the log-rank method.
Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards will be used for comparisons between groups.

For the qualitative study, all transcripts will be coded within the Nvivo software to identify themes and sentiment to establish if there is a significant difference between the two treatment modalities and their respective pathways.

sec.title: Adjusted analysis
sec.p: The main analysis will be an unadjusted analysis of the score differences. Adjustment for factors that may influence between-group differences would be explored by multivariable regression analyses. Variables to adjust for would include age at end of treatment, relapse risk (since randomisation stratified by this factor), baseline values, dose received by the OAR and distance to the rectal wall achieved by the rectal spacer.

sec.title: Interim analysis and criteria for the premature termination
sec.p: An interim analysis will take place when 50% of the participants (110 in total) have been randomised and completed 6 months of follow-up. Within this analysis, both toxicity and survival data will be reviewed. Both treatments are established standard of care treatment options with successful long-term survival data and acceptable toxicities, and therefore, it is not expected that the trial will need to be stopped early. The trial is not powered to test the significance on survival outcomes and is only powered to review meaningful differences in the EPIC-26 questionnaire.
As this study is being completed as part of a Medical Doctorate degree, an interim analysis will also take place and be written up as part of the thesis prior to study closure.

sec.title: Data collection tools and source document identification
sec.p: Electronic case report forms with details of patient demography, treatment and follow-up will be collected and managed in a purpose-built password-protected database using REDCap electronic data capture tools42 43 hosted by the Royal Surrey Scientific Computing department. The database provides an intuitive interface for validated data capture with audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export procedures. A ‘randomisation’ module will be used for centralised computer-generated allocation of patients to treatment arms and a ‘survey’ module facilitates capture of PROMs questionnaires in electronic or paper format. Paper questionnaires are transcribed in the database.

sec.title: Access to data
sec.p: Direct access will be granted to authorised representatives from the Sponsor, host institution and the regulatory authorities to permit trial-related monitoring, audits and inspections in line with participant consent.

sec.title: Archiving
sec.p: It is the sponsor’s responsibility to archive the data obtained within the study following notification to do so by the CI as per General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) guidance. All data obtained from the patient will be archived for a minimum of 5 years on completion of the study to help guide future research publications within this field.

sec.title: Monitoring
sec.p: The LDR BURST trial is an unblinded, randomised controlled trial with a simple format. Both of the treatments within the trial are standard of care treatment options and within ‘Usual Care Competence’ of the Trust. Patients will undergo thorough screening to deem suitability to each treatment option to lower the risk of treatment-related complications. Monitoring will take place throughout the trial with an experienced multidisciplinary team to ensure the trial complies with the protocol, that the rights and well-being of trial participants are protected and the reported trial data is accurate, complete and verifiable.

sec.title: Research Ethics Committee (REC) review and reports
sec.p: Any substantial amendments that require review by the REC will only be implemented once the necessary approval from the REC is obtained. Any correspondence with the REC will be clearly documented and stored within the Trial Master File.
All participants will give their informed written consent to take part in the trial.

In the unlikely event that the trial is ended early, the Chief Investigator will notify the REC. On closure of the trial, the Chief Investigator will notify the REC and a report of the study will be generated to the REC within 1 year of closure.

sec.title: Peer review
sec.p: The final trial protocol has been reviewed by two independent consultants who are experts within their respective fields and have vast experience in trial management. This invaluable feedback has helped guide the trial towards becoming a cornerstone in future literature within the prostate radiotherapy field. The trial is strongly supported by both reviewers.

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: All information provided to patients, including the PIS, consent form and follow-up questionnaires will be written in plain English using language that is clear and avoiding medical jargon. Prior to distribution, our PIS was sent to members of the Prostate Project Charity for feedback. The language was altered based on this feedback, for example, removing the word ‘study’ and replacing this with the word ‘trial’. The PIS was also updated following the REC committee review, with the addition of a flow diagram to help patients understanding of the treatment pathway.

As part of the study, there will also be a qualitative aspect with short patient interviews. From this, we hope to learn more about the similarities and differences in the patient journey and how we can improve patient care.

sec.title: Regulatory compliance
sec.p: The trial was approved by the Administration of Radioactive Substances Advisory Committee (ARSAC) on the 1st of August 2025 (ARSAC reference AA-11901).

Both treatments use ionising radiation. There is no additional dose of radiation within this trial from diagnostic imaging or treatment delivery when compared with a patient who is not on clinical trial. All procedures are compliant with the Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations, and an appropriate review by a Medical Physics Expert and Clinical Radiation Expert will take place prior to any treatment delivery.

sec.title: Data protection and patient confidentiality
sec.p: The Royal Surrey NHS Foundation Trust will act as the ‘Data Controller’ for the study. All patients will have a hospital number registering them to the Trust. Only relevant medical information will be accessed or requested by the trial team for the patient, including relevant diagnostic investigations that may have taken place from another hospital. The Data Controller will ensure that all data are processed and handled in accordance with data protection legislation. See section 9 on Data Handling for further details on how trial data will be stored.

sec.title: Indemnity
sec.p: The Royal Surrey NHS Foundation Trust maintains professional liability insurance to address the potential legal responsibilities of the sponsor and employees for any harm to NHS participants resulting from the research’s design and management. For sites outside of the UK, Royal Surrey NHS Trust as Sponsor would work with the site to ensure appropriate Insurance/Indemnity is in place.

sec.title: Amendments
sec.p: The LDR BURST study has been approved by the REC and ARSAC committee as a single centre study. We intend to expand the trial within other UK and international centres. These centres must undergo a quality assurance process set out by the host institution before joining the trial. A trial amendment will be submitted to the REC for the expansion to a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Centres that lack experience with rectal spacer gel will randomise to LDR brachytherapy versus five fraction stereotactic radiotherapy without spacer gel at the prescribed doses within the protocol. Participants without a rectal spacer gel will be evaluated as part of a dedicated subcohort analysis. Centres that do not use Gold Anchor fiducial markers as part of their SBRT delivery, or choose to omit them, may still participate provided radiotherapy can be delivered safely and accurately, subject to appropriate local quality assurance checks.
European centres, operating outside of the NHS, that wish to participate will obtain local sponsorship and ethical approval.
Any additional amendments deemed significant by the investigating team will be submitted to the REC for consideration.

sec.title: Quality assurance
sec.p: All participating sites will undergo a radiotherapy quality assurance process in which three PDF treatment plans for both LDR brachytherapy and SBRT prostate are submitted to the central site (Royal Surrey County Hospital) for review. This is to confirm compliance with the protocol dose constraints and planning standards.

sec.title: Dissemination policy
sec.p: The data obtained from the study will be submitted for presentation at National and International conferences. The data provided will help guide clinicians in future prostate cancer management. In particular, a much-needed area of research is the role of Spacer Gel which lacks randomised control data and is recommended by NICE.

As the study is part of a Medical Doctorate, the data will be analysed and submitted to the University of Surrey as part of a thesis. The study will not have completed at this point; however, the thesis will act as a welcomed interim analysis for the initial cohort of patients on trial.

The results of the study will be written and submitted to a medical journal for publishing. It is anticipated that this study will generate multiple papers given the significant amount of data it can generate to guide medical professionals. The authorship of such papers will only be from those directly involved in the trial, analysis and write-up.

fn.p: Funding: This study is being supported by The Urology Foundation (TUF) Charity following successful grant application. The LDR BURST Trial has also received a donation from the Prostate Project Charity. Teleflex, the manufacturer of Barrigel, will support the trial by supplying rectal spacer gel for all study participants and has provided a research grant to the clinical investigators.
